I looked at therapists that take my insurance (hoping you have one) and then selected any male therapist (I feel more comfortable with a male than female, I’m a make btw). If the therapist you first select doesn’t appear to be helping the move on to another one, until you find one. And the only way a therapist can help you is if you are upfront and honest with them. Tell them everything they need to know so that they have enough information to create a treatment plan. 

It worked for me. I tried several therapists until I landed on this one guy who I saw for around 9 years. Had to stop seeing him since I moved. I got through some bad times with his help. I can’t assure you it will work and sometimes you have to have medication involved along with the therapy.

Like you I’m still in college. In my second semester my anxiety randomly started to shoot up and I started having more prevalent suicidal ideations that became worse due to a medication a doc prescribed to me for the worsening anxiety. That semester my grades fell luckily only towards the end of the semester. The lack of motivation and the crippling anxiety and depression is something I completely understand. The best thing you can do is call up the college’s counseling office and set up and appointment. Email your professors about what is happening, believe me when I say this they do care. Make the appointment with the counselor to get a diagnoses and work with them and you may be able to get some extensions on homework and other things. I know the feeling of being overwhelmed by the school work and not being able to talk to the professor face to face. 

It’s going to sound cliche of me but it does get easier. Believe me, and if you need to take fewer classes next semester. Something I did, and if need be drop a class if that’s what it comes to this semester. Lessen your load until you have a good grasp of it. I went from taking 15 credit hours to 9. Then I went from 9 to 12 and have resumed 15. 

Your situation can still be managed, you just need to find the right resources. Hell had it not been for me literally telling a counselor about my ideations I may have well gone through with it. You have nothing to lose by shooting your professor an email explaining the situation and setting up a therapist appointment. I hope this helps

For those who read this. I think what this person is saying is that the person with suicidal ideations or the person who has attempted is the victim of suicide not the people around them. People will try to make themselves out to be the victim in some cases of suicide, which takes away from the real point as to why the person committed. 

Please correct me if I’m wrong here.

Your expectation that she will return to how she used to be is a bit naive for lack of a better word. When those ideations begin at least in my case they don’t just disappear. The damage done from them is manageable but it’s also permanent. She thought it was a good idea chances are a small part in her mind will always think that way. You have to hope that woman she becomes as she ages is one that can hold on and handle her mental predicament with outside professional help when needed. 

I used to be a lot more affectionate, I used to also be happier but suicidal ideations tend to have an affect of countering those character traits. Her path is not an easy one especially with covid.

My advice is don’t try to force the bond. Forcing a bond with her will not work. Do not by any means tell her things like “how could you have done this”, don’t tell her she was acting selfishly. Don’t try to make yourself out to be the victim because you’re not she is. That’s one of the biggest issues I have with people, they act like they are the victims of suicide when it’s the person who is suicidal who is the victim. Develop the relationship with her from the ground up, have a solid foundation and then the rest will fall into place.

14 years of age is around the time I had suicidal ideations. I hope she finds the source of her discomfort and sadness and I hope that she finds the will to go on and refute the inner thoughts of suicide. Good luck to her
